item.text:
**5B.10 | Tinubu in 2024**
Bottom line: **mixed, leaning negative**. The strongest 2024 evidence says Tinubu’s reforms started to improve macro indicators and fiscal buffers from a fragile baseline, but the year also produced severe household pain, inflation, protest blowback, and no clear evidence yet that the economy had actually moved onto a broadly better trajectory for ordinary Nigerians.

**Accepted claims**
- **Nigeria: 2024 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; Staff Statement; and Statement by the Executive Director for Nigeria** | IMF | 2024-05-09 | https://www.imf.org/en/publications/cr/issues/2024/05/08/nigeria-2024-article-iv-consultation-press-release-staff-report-staff-statement-and-548726  
  The IMF said Tinubu’s government had launched an ambitious stabilization program after inheriting a weak macro position, including subsidy reform, FX-window unification, revenue mobilization, and social safety nets. This is the clearest evidence that the administration was responding with a coherent policy package rather than improvisation.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

- **Staying the Course on Reforms: Progress Amidst Challenges** | World Bank | 2024-10-17 | https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/10/17/nigeria-staying-the-course-on-reforms-progress-amidst-challenges  
  The World Bank said reforms since May 2023 had produced modest growth, improved fiscal health, rising reserves, and a narrowing deficit, and that these changes had reduced debt-related risks. It explicitly described the direction as a stronger development path, though still incomplete.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

- **Nigeria Development Update, October 2024 Datasheet** | World Bank | 2024-10-17 | https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099524010162440675  
  The World Bank said Nigeria had undertaken difficult but necessary reforms to turn around a trajectory damaged by policy missteps and shocks, with positive results beginning to show in inflation, fiscal position, and reserves. This supports a conditional “yes” on trajectory, but only if reforms continue.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

- **Supporting Nigeria’s Homegrown Reforms: New World Bank Financing for Inclusive Growth and Revenue Diversification** | World Bank | 2024-06-13 | https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/06/13/supporting-nigeria-homegrown-reforms-new-world-bank-financing-for-inclusive-growth-and-revenue-diversification  
  The Bank said Nigeria had taken critical steps to restore macro stability, raise revenues, and create room for growth and poverty reduction, and that its package was meant to support a more sustainable and inclusive path. This is strong external validation of the reform direction.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9, 5B.8

- **Nigeria security forces deploy, government offers dialogue as protests loom** | Reuters via Investing.com | 2024-07-31 | https://www.investing.com/news/economic-indicators/nigeria-security-forces-deploy-government-offers-dialogue-as-protests-loom-3546462  
  Reuters reported inflation above 34% after subsidy removal, naira devaluation, and electricity tariff hikes, showing the reform path had not yet stabilized living conditions. This is evidence against a clean “stronger trajectory” verdict because the adjustment costs were still overwhelming.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

- **At least 3 killed in Nigeria at protests over high cost of living** | Reuters via Investing.com | 2024-08-01 | https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/hundreds-gather-across-nigerian-cities-to-protest-cost-of-living-crisis-3548376  
  Reuters tied nationwide protests to cost-of-living pain, governance anger, and inflation above 34%, indicating the public had not experienced the reforms as shared improvement. That weakens any claim that the economy was plainly on a better path in practice by late 2024.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9, 5B.8

- **Nigerian businesses count losses from inflation protests** | Reuters via ThePrint | 2024-08-09 | https://theprint.in/world/nigerian-businesses-count-losses-from-inflation-protests/2216016/  
  Reuters reported that the protests themselves imposed large business losses and reflected a broader collapse in purchasing power and confidence. That is not proof reforms failed structurally, but it shows the 2024 trajectory was still unstable and costly.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

- **Nigeria: 2024 is still a severe hardship year, not a full recovery** | World Bank | 2024-06-13 and 2024-10-17 | https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/feature/2024/06/13/turning-the-corner-nigeria-ongoing-path-of-economic-reforms ; https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2024/10/17/nigeria-staying-the-course-on-reforms-progress-amidst-challenges  
  Across both World Bank pieces, the recurring message is that reforms improved macro credibility but households and businesses still faced severe short-term pain, with inflation remaining high. This is the best evidence for a mixed verdict: better macro trajectory in the making, but not yet a broadly better economy.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

**Negative / limiting evidence**
- **At least 3 killed in Nigeria at protests over high cost of living** | Reuters via Investing.com | 2024-08-01 | https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/hundreds-gather-across-nigerian-cities-to-protest-cost-of-living-crisis-3548376  
  The same Reuters report shows the reforms had triggered acute social backlash, with deadly protests over hardship. That is strong evidence against a clean competence narrative for 2024 outcomes.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

- **Nigerian protests fizzle out amid deadly police crackdown** | Reuters via ThePrint | 2024-08-05 | https://theprint.in/world/nigerian-protests-fizzle-out-amid-deadly-police-crackdown/2208444/  
  Reuters described the protests as a reaction to economic hardship and noted that force and fear, not improved living conditions, ended the immediate unrest. This undercuts the idea that the economy had already improved enough to absorb shock.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

- **Nigeria: 2024 Article IV Consultation** | IMF | 2024-05-09 | https://www.imf.org/en/publications/cr/issues/2024/05/08/nigeria-2024-article-iv-consultation-press-release-staff-report-staff-statement-and-548726  
  The IMF also warned that near-term risks were tilted to the downside and that the reform package would impose hard adjustment costs. This matters because it frames 2024 less as a completed turnaround than as a fragile transition.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

- **Nigeria Development Update, October 2024 Datasheet** | World Bank | 2024-10-17 | https://documents.worldbank.org/en/publication/documents-reports/documentdetail/099524010162440675  
  The World Bank said inflation was still high and that reforms were not yet complete; it also linked the outlook to continued policy execution rather than achieved success. This limits any strong positive judgment.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

- **Nigeria | World Bank Group** | World Bank | 2025 page summarizing 2024 results, but reflecting the 2024 state of the economy | https://www.worldbank.org/ext/en/country/nigeria  
  The Bank says fiscal pressures and high debt-service costs persisted and that poverty remained high even as macro indicators improved. This supports a guarded reading: the trajectory was better on paper, but broad welfare gains had not yet arrived.  
  **QIDs:** 5B.10, 5B.9

**Search gap**
- I did not find strong direct 2024 evidence on unemployment trends specifically, beyond general job-creation language and worsening business conditions.
- I also did not find a clean 2024 source showing that debt service was materially resolved; the evidence is indirect, through narrowing deficits, higher reserves, and World Bank language about reduced debt-related risks.
- So the strongest defensible conclusion is: **Tinubu likely improved the macro trajectory at the policy and fiscal-credibility level, but by the end of 2024 the economy had not yet clearly improved on the ground for most households.**
